allocation: Existing UNATTEMPTED R11 author15 explicitly rebound to R12; no spent hold refund

all_directives.summary: System designs must maintain clear separation of concerns and well-defined component boundaries so that each part of the system is independently understandable, testable, and replaceable without cascading changes.
all_directives.title: Architectural Integrity Standard

all_directives.summary: Material technical and governance decisions must be captured with enough context that future contributors can understand why a path was chosen and what constraints must remain true.
all_directives.title: Decision Documentation Requirement

all_directives.summary: Implemented behavior and produced artifacts must remain faithful to approved specifications, with any necessary deviations explicitly documented and reviewed before acceptance.
all_directives.title: Specification Fidelity Requirement

all_directives.summary: Doctrine artifacts must be versioned with traceable change rationale so downstream consumers can understand compatibility and migration impact.
all_directives.title: Doctrine Versioning Requirement

all_directives.summary: Changes should stay close to the problem being solved to reduce blast radius, simplify review, and lower regression risk.
all_directives.title: Locality of Change

all_directives.summary: Leave touched areas in a better state by default. When an area already modified for the current task carries a failing test, lint, or type issue, fixing it is the default stance — not an optional nicety. Establishing whether a failure is pre-existing routinely costs more effort than simply fixing it, and litigating blame leaves the campground dirtier; so the default is to fix, and to defer only with an explicit rationale. At planning point-cuts (post-spec, post-plan, post-tasks), this rule extends to proactive domain-matched debt folding: if a foldable tech-debt item belongs to the current mission's primary domain, it may be incorporated into the current scope; items outside the domain boundary are filed as issues and deferred, never silently absorbed. See also DIRECTIVE_024 for locality-of-change discipline; DIRECTIVE_040 for structural intervention on recurring bugs.
all_directives.title: Boy Scout Rule

all_directives.summary: Local work should prefer efficient, low-noise tooling so investigation, editing, validation, and repository operations stay fast and reproducible across development environments.
all_directives.title: Efficient Local Tooling

all_directives.summary: Agent-authored commits must avoid GPG or SSH signing in unattended workflows so automation does not fail on missing key material or unverifiable signatures.
all_directives.title: Agent Commit Signing Policy

all_directives.summary: Code changes must pass the relevant automated tests and static validation gates before handoff so regressions and interface drift are caught early.
all_directives.title: Test and Typecheck Quality Gate

all_directives.summary: Every design decision must be made with explicit awareness of the bounded context it belongs to. Code, terminology, and abstractions must align with the context's ubiquitous language. Crossing a context boundary requires an explicit translation layer; implicit coupling across boundaries is prohibited.
all_directives.title: Context-Aware Design

all_directives.summary: Agents must never assume that shared vocabulary implies shared meaning. Before acting on any task that contains domain-specific, ambiguous, or overloaded terminology, the agent must explicitly state its interpretation of each key term and confirm that interpretation with the requester. Misaligned understanding discovered after implementation is far more costly than a brief clarification exchange before it begins.
all_directives.title: Conceptual Alignment

all_directives.summary: Agent-authored commits must stage only the expected deliverables for the current work package. Blanket staging commands that could inadvertently include unrelated changes, secrets, or build artefacts are prohibited.
all_directives.title: Targeted Staging Policy

all_directives.summary: Require test-first behavior across acceptance and implementation layers, selecting tactics based on scope and risk. Tests define the contract before production code is written.
all_directives.title: Test-First Development

all_directives.summary: Codebase-wide renames, terminology migrations, and bulk string changes must classify string occurrences by semantic context before edits begin. Different contexts (code symbols, imports, filesystem paths, serialized keys, CLI commands, docs, tests, logs) may have different change rules.
all_directives.title: Bulk Edit Occurrence Classification

all_directives.summary: Exercise the system under test through its external interfaces only, without reference to its internal code structure, implementation details, or internal paths. Test cases derive from specifications, requirements, and design parameters, and assertions are made on observable outputs returned through those external interfaces. "Black-box" refers to the technique (absence of structural knowledge) and is independent of test scope — the scope is selected separately by responsibility, not by default to end-to-end.
all_directives.title: Black-Box Integration Testing

all_directives.summary: Behavior-describing artifacts must evolve together. When observable behavior changes, the canonical examples, acceptance checks, narrative specifications, user documentation, glossary terms, code-level documentation, and architecture records must be updated in the same change so no reader is left with a stale picture of the system.
all_directives.title: Living Documentation Sync

all_directives.summary: When the SPDD/REASONS doctrine pack is active, an implementation must remain inside the approved canvas's Requirements, Operations, Norms, and Safeguards unless a deviation is explicitly recorded. Applies to implement and review actions on projects whose charter selection includes the SPDD paradigm, either REASONS canvas tactic, or this directive.
all_directives.title: Structured Prompt Change-Boundary

all_directives.summary: Constrain agentic implementation work toward test-first, strongly typed, modular, boring, reviewable code. Select this directive when the user names Lynn Cole's rules or expresses concern that coding agents produce excessive, bloated, clever, over-abstracted, or hard-to-review code.
all_directives.title: Lynn Cole Engineering Culture

all_directives.summary: When a bug class has recurred and prior reactive point-fixes have not stopped the chain, the next response must be a structural intervention that closes the class — not another point fix. Use the five-paradigm parallel-debugging tactic to identify the structural root cause, enumerate dormant masks, and author one fix plan that closes the whole class.
all_directives.title: Recurring-Bug Structural-Intervention Discipline

all_directives.summary: Tests must protect change, not obstruct it. A test earns its place by failing exactly when the contract is violated and passing otherwise. Tests that pass for the wrong reason (mocked-out behavior, tautological or wiring-only assertions) or fail on correct, behavior-neutral changes (implementation-coupled assertions, line-pinned ratchets) are friction: they hide regressions and pressure engineers to revert good changes.
all_directives.title: Tests as Scaffold, Not Friction

all_directives.summary: Documentation is governed, single-source-of-truth content, not a wiki. Every documentation file lives under the single Common Docs root, declares its own lifecycle metadata in in-file frontmatter, and is curated under a delete-stale policy. This directive binds the conventions decided in the Common Docs reconciliation ADR (2026-06-27) so they are enforced by live checks rather than remembered by authors.
all_directives.title: Common Docs Documentation Standard

all_directives.summary: A repeating defect class signals a missing structural constraint. The correct response is to eliminate the recurrence path with a structural mechanism — an AST call-site gate, a type invariant, or a shrink-only ratchet — rather than adding another process rule or discipline reminder. Structural enforcement closes the class permanently; process rules merely defer the next occurrence.
all_directives.title: Close Defect Classes by Construction

all_directives.summary: Agents and operators must use the canonical doctrine template, skill, or CLI command rather than improvising a substitute or copying from a prior mission artifact, because older artifacts drift from the canonical surface and copying them propagates the drift. When a concept is found to live in more than one location (a split-brain surface), the correct response is to consolidate to a single canonical authority — not to add the same behavior to every copy. A documented CLI command that is absent from the running tool is a gap to file upstream, not an invitation to hand-roll a workaround.
all_directives.title: Canonical Sources and Unification

all_directives.summary: All changes to the remote main branch go through pull requests — agents never push directly or merge without explicit operator instruction. Before executing any high-risk git operation (merge, rebase, deletion, force operations), agents must read the mission spec and current context first. Neither rule may be bypassed under time pressure or assumed from a task title alone.
all_directives.title: PRs-Only and Read-Intent Before High-Risk Operations

all_directives.summary: Every mission branch and pull request an agent prepares must be readable, consistent, and independently reviewed before it is handed to the operator. Concretely, three properties are required and must not be traded away for speed: (1) LINEAR history — the branch is rebased onto the current upstream base and carries a small set of logically-sliced commits, never a tangle of merge and status commits (rebase over merge); (2) CONSISTENT and COMPLETE scope — the branch finishes the work it set out to do and does not defer genuinely small remaining items to a follow-up, deferring only work that is genuinely high-effort or mission-sized; (3) INDEPENDENTLY REVIEWED — the aggregate diff has had an independent review before, or in parallel to, opening the draft PR, with real findings folded in while the PR is still a draft. The adversarial review squad (adversarial-squad-deployment) is the RECOMMENDED review mechanism — not a mandated gate; it stays optional per its own doctrine.
all_directives.title: Readable and Consistent Pull Requests

all_directives.summary: Any artifact intended for a human reader must be tailored to a named, identifiable audience rather than written for an undefined or generic reader. Identifying who the reader is, what they already know, and what they need from the artifact must happen before drafting, not after. Artifacts that skip this step tend to over-explain to experts, under-explain to newcomers, or bury the point the reader actually needs.
all_directives.title: Audience-Oriented Writing

all_directives.summary: Any agent operation that reads, cites, or reasons about a versioned artifact (a glossary, a specification, a doctrine element, a released document) must reference the current canonical version, not a cached or stale copy. Analysis performed against a stale version produces confidently wrong conclusions - it is not merely lower-quality, it is actively misleading because it looks complete.
all_directives.title: Version Governance

all_directives.summary: Before beginning substantive work, an agent with a defined specialist identity (as opposed to a generic assistant) should open with a short role/scope declaration - who it is, what it is about to do, and any hard constraint it operates under - so the human or the requesting agent can catch a mismatch (wrong agent invoked, wrong scope assumed) before work is wasted rather than after. This is advisory guidance, not a runtime gate: no mechanism blocks work when the declaration is absent.
all_directives.title: Agent Declaration and Self-Introduction

all_directives.summary: Any agent operation that uses an authentication credential (token, key, password, session cookie) to call an external system must never log, echo, or otherwise surface that credential in output, error messages, or artifacts. The discipline is prevention-first: the credential must be kept out of any surface that could be logged or written in the first place, rather than surfaced and then scrubbed after the fact.
all_directives.title: Credential Handling Discipline

all_directives.summary: Install-time and dependency-resolution decisions must be evaluated against a threat-CLASS model, not a static package denylist. Worm-style supply-chain compromises (credential-harvesting postinstall scripts, typosquatted or namespace-confused packages, rapid-republish attacks during an active incident window) recur across ecosystems faster than any hand-maintained list of bad package/version pairs can track. Agents and mission workflows must therefore default to five threat-class controls for every dependency addition or upgrade: (1) official registry authenticity — the resolved package and version must come from the approved official registry, not an unexpected mirror or namespace; (2) package freshness visibility — first-publish and latest-publish/update timestamps must be surfaced so an operator can see when a version is suspiciously new or was substantially reworked; (3) deny-by-default lifecycle-script approval — `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` scripts are never auto-approved and must be explicitly allowlisted with a documented justification when required for legitimate native builds; (4) Node Active LTS awareness — the project/runtime Node version is checked against current Active LTS and any skew is explicitly disclosed with rationale, never silently accepted; (5) incident-list and IoC/persistence posture — known active-incident package/version lists and indicator-of-compromise (IoC) or persistence patterns (unexpected postinstall network calls, credential/token exfiltration attempts, self-propagating install scripts) are treated as class-level risk signals to check for, with CAS/vendor incident feeds as the external authority of record — this directive never hardcodes specific incident package names or versions as core truth, because that list changes faster than doctrine can be re-authored.
all_directives.title: Supply-Chain Install Safety

all_directives.summary: Refactoring is behaviour-preserving restructuring, and it stays safe only when it is disciplined. Change the shape of the code in small, individually reversible steps while a green test suite holds behaviour constant; never fold a behaviour change into the same step as a structural move. Before touching the code, name the smell the move addresses — feature envy, a long method, a data clump, duplicated logic, a conditional switching on state — so the improvement is aimed at a stated problem rather than at taste. Apply exactly one transformation at a time and re-run the tests after each, so that when a step goes red the cause is unambiguous and the step can be reverted on its own. This directive governs HOW to restructure once a smell is identified; the concrete moves it recommends (extract, encapsulate, move, replace-conditional-with- polymorphism, incremental replacement) are the refactoring tactics, each chosen by the specific smell it resolves.
all_directives.title: Disciplined Refactoring

all_directives.summary: Locality of Change (DIRECTIVE_024), the Boy Scout Rule (DIRECTIVE_025), and the Change Apply Smallest Viable Diff tactic each bound the size of a change from a different angle, and by design they are not fully compatible: Locality of Change minimizes blast radius, Boy Scout Rule licenses opportunistic in-place improvement of touched areas, and smallest-viable-diff minimizes the diff itself. This directive gives an operator or agent a single place to weigh the three together on a given change, instead of applying each in isolation, so the default doctrine pack stays coherent even though the underlying tension between the three rules is real and intentionally left unresolved at the rule level.
all_directives.title: Reconciling Change-Scope Tensions

all_directives.summary: Document and reason about a system's architecture with the C4 model's progressive zoom — System Context, then Container, then Component, then Code — so every diagram serves one audience at one level of detail instead of a single all-in-one picture that serves nobody. Draw only the levels that earn their keep: a Context diagram is almost always worth it, Container diagrams for systems with more than one deployable unit, Component diagrams only for containers with non-obvious internal structure, and Code-level diagrams only when they can be generated cheaply. Keep every diagram in a text-based, version-controlled form (Mermaid or PlantUML diagram-as-code, not a binary export) so it diffs, reviews, and travels with the code it describes. This directive is an extensible HUB for architecture-documentation techniques: the C4 zoom-in workflow, the diagram review checklist, the diagram-as-code toolguides, the drill-down abstraction-level discipline, and code/documentation analysis for boundary discovery all hang off it, and further techniques are wired in as they are supplied. It governs HOW to document and reason about architecture at the right zoom level; the concrete techniques it recommends are the suggested members, each chosen for the specific documentation need it serves.
all_directives.title: Use C4 Model Techniques

all_directives.summary: Line and branch coverage prove a test executed a piece of code; they do not prove a test would notice if that code were wrong. Mutation testing closes that gap: it introduces small, deliberate faults (mutants) into the code under test and asks whether the existing tests fail. A surviving mutant is a concrete, located piece of evidence that some assertion does not actually pin the behaviour it appears to cover — the tests run the line but do not constrain its outcome. Use mutation testing to find those hollow assertions and strengthen them until the mutant is killed. Treat the mutation score as a QUALITY SIGNAL that points at weak spots, never as a target to be gamed: a number driven up by suppressing awkward mutants, over-fitting tests to implementation detail, or asserting on incidental output teaches nothing and rots the suite. Because a full-suite mutation run is expensive, run it on the CHANGED SCOPE under review — the modules a work package touched — rather than the whole tree, so the signal is timely and the survivors it surfaces are the ones a reviewer can act on now. This directive is an extensible HUB for mutation-testing technique: the run/triage workflow, the mutation-aware test-design conventions, and the language-specific mutation toolguides all hang off it.
all_directives.title: Use Mutation Testing to Validate Test Quality

all_directives.summary: Preserve original WP 5.1 native and companion formats in both missions; Wordling 5.2 is not a file-format version. Follow docs/compatibility.md.
all_directives.title: Original format permanently

all_directives.summary: M1 delivers complete plain WP 5.1 DOS parity. M2 begins after M1 acceptance and adds PDF export and selected conveniences. See docs/roadmap.md.
all_directives.title: Parity before modernization

all_directives.summary: No-edit saves are byte-identical. Edits preserve unrelated content. Unknown data is preserved or unsafe edits/saves are refused before replacing the original.
all_directives.title: Lossless and safe saves

all_directives.summary: Track manual discovery, section study, original-app observation, implementation, and differential verification separately. Declare exact reference release and resources.
all_directives.title: Evidence before compatibility claims

all_directives.summary: Implement the application in Go using Bubble Tea. Keep terminal rendering independent of document and layout semantics.
all_directives.title: Go and Bubble Tea on Linux

all_directives.summary: Changed Go code passes formatting, build, go test ./..., go vet ./...; binary readers need malformed-input and fuzz tests; writers need original-app checks. Do not redistribute proprietary references without permission.
all_directives.title: Verification and provenance

all_directives.summary: Inventory all original functionality including utilities and platform-dependent behavior. Record explicit Linux adaptations and owner-approved scope decisions; do not silently omit difficult features.
all_directives.title: Complete coverage stays visible

directive_references.name: Decision Documentation Requirement
directive_references.rationale: Every requirement must be traceable to a source artifact with decision rationale

directive_references.name: Audience-Oriented Writing
directive_references.rationale: Specifications and acceptance criteria must be tailored to a named audience (domain expert vs. implementer)

directive_references.name: Conceptual Alignment
directive_references.rationale: Confirm domain terms are understood consistently before formalizing requirements

mode_defaults.use_case: Translating informal requirements, mapping user journeys, identifying edge cases
Writing Given/When/Then scenarios, encoding acceptance criteria

specialization.avoidance_boundary: Does not make implementation decisions, architecture choices, or framework selections. Does not perform datamodel analysis, field-level mapping, or entity-relationship work — that is a datamodel specialist's domain. Does not hand off specifications before acceptance criteria are unambiguous and formally expressed. Does not proceed into implementation planning.
specialization.primary_focus: Functional description to specification translation: formalising informal requirements into structured specs with unambiguous acceptance criteria and BDD scenarios (Given/When/Then). User journey mapping: identifying actors, system boundaries, happy paths, alternate paths, and edge cases. Regulatory requirement translation: grounding specifications in cited product and regulatory documentation before formalising. Producing handoff-ready artifacts — feature files or structured AC documents — that implementation agents can consume without further clarification.
specialization.secondary_awareness: Regulatory and product context relevant to the domain at hand. Engagement and ticketing context from the project's requirements-tracking tools. Traceability chain from source requirement to acceptance criterion to test to implementation. Signals for when to escalate to a datamodel specialist (entity-level, field-level, or schema-level questions) or to Architect Alphonso (structural or cross-system design questions).
specialization.success_definition: Every requirement is traceable to a source artifact. Acceptance criteria are formal, encodable (Given/When/Then), and independently executable. Edge cases and alternate flows are explicitly documented. Implementation agents can begin work without further clarification from Annie or the domain expert.
